title: Washington Just Struck Iran Again and Killed Its Oil License. India's Brief Energy Relief May Already Be Over.
excerpt: Brent crude surges past $76 as the US retaliates for Hormuz tanker attacks and revokes Tehran's right to sell oil — adding $12.6 billion to India's annual import bill if prices hold
body:
Key Takeaways
  • US military strikes against Iran escalate tensions in the Persian Gulf.
  • Brent crude oil prices surged over 5%, reaching nearly $76 per barrel.
  • India's annual energy import bill could increase by $12.6 billion.
  • The US revoked Iran's oil sales license, threatening the fragile ceasefire.
  • India's currency faces pressure as oil prices rise and current account deficit widens.
The brief window of calm in the Persian Gulf is over. The United States launched a new wave of military strikes against Iran late on Tuesday and revoked a license that had allowed Tehran to sell oil on international markets — a one-two punch that sent oil prices surging more than 5 per cent and put the fragile US-Iran ceasefire under its most severe pressure yet. The escalation came after Iran fired at three commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz over a 24-hour span on Monday and Tuesday, including a massive Qatari liquefied natural gas tanker and a Saudi-flagged crude oil supertanker. "Iran's demonstrated aggression was unwarranted, dangerous, and a clear violation of the ceasefire," US Central Command said in a statement. ## What Just Happened US forces struck Iranian air defence systems, coastal surveillance infrastructure, surface-to-air missile batteries, anti-ship cruise missile sites, and drone launch facilities across southern Iran. Iranian media reported explosions in the port cities of Bandar Abbas and Sirik, as well as on Qeshm Island — all strategic military locations that have been hit multiple times since the war began in February. Hours earlier, the US Treasury Department revoked a general license issued on 22 June that had permitted Iran to sell crude oil and petroleum products on the global market through 21 August. Buyers now have until 17 July to wind down existing transactions. The license was a centrepiece of the ceasefire agreement and its removal strips Tehran of the economic lifeline it won at the negotiating table. Brent crude jumped to nearly $76 a barrel — up from about $70 earlier in the week — marking the sharpest single-day move since the ceasefire was announced in April. > **""Iran's demonstrated aggression was unwarranted, dangerous, and a clear violation of the ceasefire," US Central Command said in a statement."** ## Why India Cannot Look Away The timing could not be worse for New Delhi. India had just lifted emergency gas restrictions two days ago, banking on the ceasefire holding and oil prices staying near pre-war levels. That calculation is now under direct threat. India imports roughly 88 per cent of its crude oil, and nearly two-thirds of those barrels pass through the Strait of Hormuz. Every dollar added to the price of Brent costs the Indian economy roughly $2.1 billion annually in additional import bills. A sustained move from $70 to $76 would add approximately $12.6 billion to India's annual energy bill. The rupee, already under pressure from corporate arbitrage flows between the onshore and non-deliverable forward markets, slid past 95.47 per dollar on Monday — its weakest level in three weeks. A spike in oil prices on top of that pressure threatens to widen India's current account deficit and put additional strain on the currency. ![Persian Gulf — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/be/PersianGulf_vue_satellite_du_golfe_persique.jpg/3840px-PersianGulf_vue_satellite_du_golfe_persique.jpg) For the nine million Indians living and working in the Gulf states — in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Oman, Bahrain, and Kuwait — the escalation raises familiar anxieties about regional stability that have become a recurring feature of life since the war began. ## The Ceasefire Is Fraying The US-Iran memorandum of understanding, signed in April, was meant to create a 60-day window for negotiations on a permanent peace deal. Under the agreement, Iran pledged to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and halt attacks on commercial shipping, while Washington offered sanctions relief and a pause in military operations.

But Iran has repeatedly fired on vessels transiting the strait, claiming they violated routing rules that Tehran unilaterally imposed. The United States maintains that the strait is an international waterway where Iran has no authority to restrict maritime traffic. Indirect negotiations between the two sides in Doha, Qatar last week ended without progress. Iran's foreign ministry said on Wednesday that Tehran would "take any measure it deemed necessary to safeguard its interests and national security." President Trump, speaking from the NATO summit in Ankara, put it more bluntly: "We're either going to make a deal or we're going to finish the job. We can knock down their bridges in one hour, we can knock out their energy supply." ## What Comes Next The immediate question is whether this latest escalation breaks the ceasefire entirely or serves as another in a series of tit-for-tat exchanges that both sides step back from. For India, the stakes are concrete. The Reserve Bank of India has been intervening in currency markets to prevent a sharp rupee slide, but its ability to do so diminishes if oil prices stay elevated. India's petroleum ministry had just last week indicated it was considering further easing of fuel-price controls — a plan that now looks premature.
Timeline of Recent US-Iran Tensions

US-Iran ceasefire agreement signed.
June 22, 2023
Iran granted license to sell oil.
July 17, 2023
Deadline for winding down oil transactions.
July 2023
US military strikes against Iran commence.
The diplomatic channel between Washington and Tehran remains open, at least nominally. But with oil sanctions reimposed, US strikes escalating, and hundreds of thousands of Iranians in the streets chanting for revenge, the path from ceasefire to permanent peace just got considerably longer. *Sources: Reuters, CNN, USA Today, US Central Command, US Treasury Department*
